# Distill Performance Evidence

This directory contains retained `entire brain distill` performance artifacts.
The current retained manifest is scoped to this repository and a deterministic
local command agent. It proves the local extraction scheduler and evidence gate:
`--jobs 4` preserves the same output summary as `--jobs 1` while improving the
measured extraction-heavy wall time on a temporary copy of the current
`entire-brain` local brain.

Evidence must be collected on the repo whose performance claim it supports, or
the release copy must scope the claim to the measured repo. The committed
current-repo artifacts must not be reused to support a frontend/entire.io 24h
distill claim. That claim still needs retained dry-run and timed artifacts from
the target large session repo.

A release-citable `manifest.json` in this directory must name:

- `target.repo`, `target.repo_key`, `target.source_head`,
  `target.brain_manifest_sha256`, and `target.claim_scope`, so the measured repo
  and the release claim it supports are explicit and audit-visible;
- one `entire brain distill --dry-run --json` artifact captured before the timed
  runs;
- one serial timed `entire brain distill --json --jobs 1` artifact;
- one parallel timed `entire brain distill --json --jobs N` artifact from the
  same target repo/cache state, same agent/model/effort, same branch/force/
  max-chunk-bytes settings, and zero failed chunks;
- `artifact_sha256` entries for the three retained JSON artifacts;
- `commands` arrays with the exact retained command tokens for dry-run, serial,
  and parallel runs. Use an explicit `--agent`; do not rely on `auto`. Include
  the chosen `--max-chunk-bytes` so the chunking/call-count tradeoff is
  inspectable;
- `local_ollama_contract`, a retained non-cached `go test -json` artifact proving
  the fake loopback Ollama distill path sends the selected model to
  `/api/generate`, avoids the `ollama` PATH binary, and rejects non-loopback or
  redirected egress without requiring a real external model. This section must
  include the artifact hash, exact command, source head, source path list, and
  required test names;
- a `min_speedup` threshold greater than `1.0`.

For current retained evidence, `claim_scope` is intentionally narrow:
`current-repo local command-agent distill extraction scheduling speedup`. The
local command agent is committed as `local-command-agent.py`; it exercises
extraction, reconciliation, deterministic writes, and timing evidence without a
hosted model or network. It does not validate fact quality or hosted-model
latency. The retained `go-test-internal-cli-ollama-distill.jsonl` artifact is a
separate local-model contract proof: it exercises fake loopback Ollama with
`-count=1`, but it is not evidence that any specific Ollama model produces good
facts.

The retained timed pair is the MEDIAN of five back-to-back `--jobs 1`/`--jobs 4`
pairs collected on one machine, chosen by that rule before the runs were read.
The five spanned 2.5747x-2.6284x (median 2.5934x, stdev 0.026) against the
`min_speedup` floor of 1.25.

Run `mise run distill:evidence` after committing artifacts. The validator fails
if artifact hashes or command provenance do not match, the dry-run has missing
transcripts or warnings, branch totals do not add up, run configs differ,
cache-hit counts do not match, warnings or failed chunks are present,
serial/parallel output summaries differ, reconcile calls exceed the dry-run
upper bound, timing components exceed `total_seconds`, the parallel run uses
only one effective job, the retained command omits the artifact's
`max_chunk_bytes`, the retained fake-Ollama contract artifact is missing/stale or
lacks a required passing test, or the observed `total_seconds` speedup does not
meet the manifest threshold.

content.text:
**No measurable difference between the released binary and main — the slowness is not a regression.**

Setup: latest release `v0.1.0-nightly.202610190636` (cut from `0f1cef8d` this morning) vs main (`9943a3d7`) built with the same release flags (`CGO_ENABLED=0 -trimpath -ldflags "-s -w"`). Each run did a full `--force` distill of this repo's brain (273 sessions, 1.69 GB raw transcripts, 327 chunks) on an isolated APFS clone of the brain store, using the repo's deterministic `local-command-agent.py` so agent latency is constant. Three interleaved runs per binary.

| | released (3 runs) | main (3 runs) |
|---|---|---|
| wall time | 92 / 141 / 127 s | 91 / 136 / 75 s |
| pipeline `total_seconds` | 20.6 / 17.0 / 16.6 | 22.7 / 24.7 / 16.7 |
| facts / agent calls | 2590 / 607 | 2590 / 607 (identical) |

- Run-to-run noise (75–141 s for identical work) dwarfs any binary delta, and wall vs internal timings point in opposite directions. The distill code is also unchanged since the nightly — the ~30 commits on top are setup-UI/progress work.
- **Surprising finding:** `distill --json` reports `total_seconds` of ~17–25 s, but the command actually takes 75–141 s of wall time. Extraction (2.2 s) + reconcile (8–13 s) + write (0.5 s) account for the reported number; the other ~60–120 s — mostly scanning/preprocessing the 1.69 GB of raw transcripts — is invisible in the summary. If initial distillation feels slow, that unreported scan/preprocess phase (plus real-agent call latency, 607 calls here) is where the time goes, not a released-vs-main difference.
- Caveat: the deterministic command agent measures the CLI pipeline only. With a real agent (claude-code/codex), the 607 agent calls dominate and are binary-independent.

Artifacts are in `/tmp/distill-bench/runs/*/result.json` (delete `/tmp/distill-bench` when done). I recorded the result and the `total_seconds` gotcha as a Brain fact. If you want, I can profile the scan/preprocess phase next to see what makes the initial pass slow in absolute terms.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/evisdrenova/.claude/plugins/cache/entire-skills/entire/0.7.2/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

Entire Address Findings:

Trail 4301 targets `gh/entirehq/entire.io`, but this workspace is `entire-brain` and there's no entire.io checkout on this machine (`~/conductor/workspaces/entire.io` is empty), so I can't edit code or resolve findings from here. There are **2 open findings** (both medium, both from review agents):

1. `api/src/routes/repo-memories.ts:162` — when repo metadata omits `capabilities`, `canPush` falls back to `permission === "write"`, so a push-capable **admin** gets "Ask a repo admin" instead of onboarding/get-involved CTAs.
2. `frontend/src/routes/.../memories/index.tsx:341` — the facets query now carries viewer-specific CTA state but is keyed only by repo and isn't evicted on logout; after a user switch the previous viewer's CTA state can show until refetch.

To fix them: open an entire.io workspace in Conductor (or `entire trail checkout 4301` in an entire.io clone) and run `/address-findings` there. I left both findings open.

---

**Distillation profiling results**

Cold full distill of this repo's brain (273 sessions, 327 chunks, 1.69 GB raw transcripts, deterministic command agent, 57s wall):

| Phase | Time | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-engine: entity-provenance resolver | **~42s** | **73%** |
| Engine: extraction + reconcile + writes | ~15s | 26% |
| Startup + exit | <1s | — |

**The bottleneck is before distillation starts.** A goroutine dump 20s into the "silent" phase shows the main goroutine in `newEntityProvenanceResolver → loadEntityIndexView → sessionIDsByCheckpoint → loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly → checkpointBlobReader.read → catFileWithPolicy`, i.e. reading checkpoint metadata blobs with **one serial `git cat-file` subprocess per blob** (`internal/cli/export.go:2761`). Thousands of short-lived git execs ≈ 42 seconds, during which:

- the user sees nothing — it runs after the "distill sessions" header with no progress;
- `--json total_seconds` never counts it (the timer starts inside `runDistillForBrain`, after the resolvers — that's the wall-vs-reported gap from the earlier benchmark);
- it holds the distill pass lock, and a code comment calls it "cheap and bounded" (`distill_cmd.go:805`).

Inside the engine the profile is healthy: agent-call wait 2s (parallel, jobs 4), serial reconcile 7.4s, writes 0.5s; the biggest CPU user is transcript JSON parsing in the prefetcher (`preprocessTranscriptForDistill`, 28% of the process's 16.8s CPU), fully overlapped with agent calls. With a real agent the 607 calls dominate instead — but the 42s resolver cost stays as fixed overhead either way.

Fix candidates, in impact order: batch the blob reads through one `git cat-file --batch` process; cache the checkpoint-snapshot join (it rebuilds on every distill, even when the entity-index cache hits); and surface the phase in progress/`total_seconds` so it stops looking like a hang. Recorded in Brain (`architecture.distill.bottleneck`); benchmark artifacts in `/tmp/distill-bench/runs/`. This affects released and main equally — the code is identical in both.

content.text:
**Yes — the bottleneck is the same in the new git-backed mode, and the engine phase gets ~1.8× slower on top of it.**

I built a genuinely new-mode brain (fresh `refresh sessions` in an isolated env → `transcript_storage: "checkpoint"`, zero materialized transcripts) and reran the identical distill benchmark, with a git shim counting every subprocess:

| Same corpus, command agent, jobs 4 | old (transcript cache) | new (git-backed, COR-2128) |
|---|---|---|
| wall | 57s | 76s |
| pre-engine silent phase | ~42s | ~49s |
| engine (`total_seconds`) | 15.4s | 27.4s |
| extraction wait | 2.2s | 3.9s |
| `git cat-file` calls during distill | ~2,200 | ~2,772 |

- **The 42–49s pre-engine phase is untouched by the new mode.** It's the entity-provenance join (`sessionIDsByCheckpoint → loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly`), which reads checkpoint metadata blobs one serial `git cat-file` at a time — upstream of where transcripts live, and it repeats on warm reruns in both modes.
- **The new mode adds the same pathology to the engine:** every transcript read becomes a `git config -z` + `git cat-file` subprocess pair plus zlib decompress instead of a file read — engine time 15s → 27s, extraction wait nearly doubled.
- **The new initial flow pays the pattern a third time:** `refresh sessions` itself took 94s with ~2,486 serial cat-files before distill even starts. So a cold start in the new world is ~94s export + ~76s distill ≈ 170s, of which useful agent-call work is ~30s.

The structural fix is the same everywhere: every logical git read spawns two processes, ~5,000 spawns per phase on this repo. Routing checkpoint blob reads through one long-lived `git cat-file --batch` process (or caching the provenance join) would collapse the dominant cost in export, pre-engine, and the new read path at once. With a real agent the engine delta matters less (agent latency dominates), but the fixed ~50s pre-engine scan and 94s export are pure overhead in every mode.

Recorded in Brain under `architecture.distill.bottleneck`; artifacts in `/tmp/distill-bench/runs/{newmode-1,oldmode-shim}/`.

content.text:
Here's the full anatomy of the silent phase, now pinned down end to end:

**What it is:** building the *entity-provenance resolver* — a join that maps each session to the checkpoints/commits it touched, so new facts get anchored to the right commit. It runs inside the distill pass lock, after the "distill sessions" header, before the engine timer starts (`runDistill.func3` → `newEntityProvenanceResolver`, `internal/cli/distill_cmd.go:811`).

**The sequence** (goroutine dump + git-shim timeline + code):

1. **t≈0–0.5s** — resolve repo, storage paths, acquire the pass lock, print the header. Fast.
2. **t≈0.5s → ~43s (unshimmed)** — `loadEntityIndexView → sessionIDsByCheckpoint → loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly → readCheckpointSnapshotMetadata`: walks the checkpoint aggregate branch `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` — **2,095 checkpoint commits, 6,686 tree entries** in this repo — and reads each checkpoint's `metadata.json` blob with its own `git cat-file` subprocess, each preceded by its own `git config -z` subprocess. The shim log shows a perfectly flat ~34 reads/sec for 66 straight seconds (shimmed): ~2,200 cat-files, ~4,400 process spawns, ~29ms each, strictly serial — the main goroutine sits in `exec.Cmd.Wait` the whole time.
3. **last ~2s** — `sessionBranchByID` (parse the 1.5MB manifest), `newCheckpointCommitResolver` (one `git log --all --grep`, 0.04s), and a handful of `rev-list` calls for branch reachability.
4. Then `runDistillForBrain` starts and `total_seconds` begins counting.

**Why it hurts more than it should:**

- **Serial, two spawns per read.** ~29ms × 2,200 for data git could stream from one `cat-file --batch` process in well under a second — the blobs are small JSON.
- **Paid on every distill run.** The entity-index cache can hit, but `finish()` re-runs the session join unconditionally ("git metadata can be unchanged while sessions arrive"), and my warm reruns confirm the scan repeats — it's not a first-run-only cost.
- **Invisible.** No progress line, excluded from `total_seconds`, and it holds the distill pass lock while running.
- **It's a recurring motif, not one bug.** The same per-checkpoint cat-file walk runs again in `refresh sessions` (~2,486 calls, 94s) and in the new mode's transcript-store resolution/reads. The code comment at the call site says "reading the derived index is cheap and bounded" — true for the index file, false for the join behind it.

**Evaluation angles, impact order:** (1) route checkpoint blob reads through one long-lived `git cat-file --batch`; (2) cache the per-checkpoint metadata keyed by the aggregate branch tip — checkpoint content is immutable and content-addressed, so the cache never invalidates mid-branch; (3) skip the `config -z` preflight per call; (4) give the phase a progress line and include it in `total_seconds` so it's measurable in the field.

Want me to file this as a Linear issue (with the numbers and stack traces), or start on the `cat-file --batch` fix in this workspace?

input.title: Distill spends ~75% of wall time in a serial per-checkpoint `git cat-file` scan before the engine starts
input.description:
## Problem

On the entire-brain repo (2,095 checkpoints, 273 sessions), a full `entire brain distill --force` spends ~42s of a 57s run before `runDistillForBrain` starts. The user sees the "distill sessions" header and then silence; `--json total_seconds` never includes this time because the timer starts inside the engine.

A goroutine dump 20s into the silent phase shows the main goroutine in:

```
runDistill.func3 (distill_cmd.go:811)
→ newEntityProvenanceResolver
→ loadEntityIndexView → finish() → sessionIDsByCheckpoint
→ loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly → loadLocalCheckpointUnionSnapshot
→ readCheckpointSnapshotMetadata → checkpointBlobReader.read
→ catFileWithPolicy → runCheckpointGitLocal → exec.Cmd.Wait
```

It reads each checkpoint's `metadata.json` blob from `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` with one `git cat-file` subprocess per blob, each preceded by a `git config -z` subprocess. A git-exec shim measured a flat ~34 reads/s for the whole phase: ~2,200 cat-files, ~4,400 process spawns, ~29ms per serialized read.

## Measurements (2026-10-19, M-series mac, deterministic command agent, jobs 4)

| run | wall | pre-engine | engine (`total_seconds`) | git cat-file calls |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| distill, materialized transcripts | 57s | ~42s | 15.4s | ~2,200 |
| distill, checkpoint-backed transcripts (COR-2128) | 76s | ~49s | 27.4s | ~2,772 |
| `refresh sessions` (checkpoint-backed export) | 94s | — | — | ~2,486 |

- The scan repeats on every distill run, warm or cold: the entity-index cache can hit, but `loadEntityIndexView.finish()` re-runs the session join unconditionally.
- COR-2128 checkpoint-backed brains pay the same per-blob exec pattern again for transcript reads (engine time 15s → 27s, extraction wait 2.2s → 3.9s) and a third time in `refresh sessions`.
- The phase holds the distill pass lock and emits no progress.
- Released nightly and main perform identically; this is not a regression.

## Fix candidates (impact order)

1. Route checkpoint blob reads through one long-lived `git cat-file --batch` process instead of one exec per blob. The blobs are small JSON; batched, this phase should drop from ~42s to well under a second. Applies to the provenance join, the transcript store, and export alike.
2. Cache the per-checkpoint metadata join keyed by the `entire/checkpoints/v1` tip. Checkpoint content is immutable and content-addressed, so the cache never invalidates mid-branch.
3. Drop the `git config -z` preflight per call (halves spawns even without batching).
4. Add a progress line for the phase and include it in `total_seconds` so the cost is visible in the field.

## Repro

Benchmark harness and artifacts: `/tmp/distill-bench/` (isolated `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_*_DIR`, APFS-cloned brain store, deterministic agent `benchmarks/agent-brain/evidence/distill-perf/local-command-agent.py`). Goroutine dump: `GOTRACEBACK=all` + SIGQUIT ~20s into a run. Brain facts: `architecture.distill.bottleneck`.

**Different cache entirely — and I've now tested the cold path directly.**

**Q1: Was the 17s result a warm first run?** The 82.7s→17.0s comparison had a warm *metadata* cache (the brain had been exported before). I just reran the patched binary with the cache file deleted: **80.8s, ~2,200 cat-files — the full old behavior comes back** (output still identical). So the speedup depends entirely on that cache. That's safe for a true first-time run, though: distill refuses to run until sessions are exported, and the sessions export itself builds and saves this cache (`export.go:177–199`; my fresh isolated env confirmed `refresh sessions` created it). So a new machine pays the blob scan **once, in export** (the 94s I measured), and every distill after that reads the cache. The only way distill goes cold is a pre-cache-era brain or manually deleting the file, and then it degrades to the old scan, not an error.

**Q2: Relation to the removed transcript cache — different caches:**

- **Transcript cache (removed by COR-2128):** the 1.6GB of materialized `full.jsonl` *content* files under `<brain>/sessions/`. Gone; transcripts now stream from git checkpoint refs on demand.
- **Checkpoint metadata cache (what my fix uses):** `export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz`, ~2.7MB gzip'd, OID-keyed copies of each checkpoint's small `metadata.json` (session membership, timestamps). It survived COR-2128 — in fact COR-2128 made it *more* load-bearing, because the transcript store resolves session→checkpoint locations through this same cache (`transcript_store.go:233`). My fix just gives the distill provenance join the same cache the transcript store and export already use.

What remains uncached is transcript **content**. On the checkpoint-backed brain the patched binary runs 33.0s: pre-engine drops to ~1s, but 572 `cat-file` calls remain — those are the actual transcript chunk reads. Caching those would just reintroduce the transcript cache COR-2128 deleted; the right fix there (and for the export-side first scan) is one long-lived `git cat-file --batch` process instead of a subprocess per blob. Both validation rows are appended to COR-2182.

content.text:
One changed call site in `internal/cli/entities_cmd.go` (`sessionIDsByCheckpoint`, the join distill builds before it starts):

```diff
-	if snapshot, _, err := loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly(..., nil); err == nil && snapshot != nil {
+	metadataCache := loadCheckpointMetadataCache(filepath.Join(brainDir, filepath.FromSlash(checkpointMetadataCachePath)))
+	if snapshot, _, err := loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly(..., metadataCache); err == nil && snapshot != nil {
```

It was passing `nil` where a `*checkpointMetadataCache` belongs. That nil had two effects downstream:

1. The snapshot loader skips OID resolution when the cache is nil, so every checkpoint's `metadata.json` was read with its own `git cat-file` subprocess (~2,200 of them, serially).
2. Even though export maintains a cache of exactly these blobs (`export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz`, 2.7MB), this path never looked at it.

The fix loads that cache read-only — same pattern the transcript store already uses at `transcript_store.go:233` — and passes it through. Cache hit → blob reads become map lookups; cache miss → falls back to the old per-blob `cat-file` with identical output. Export remains the only writer of the cache file.

Every \`entire brain distill\` run spent most of its wall time before the engine started: \`sessionIDsByCheckpoint\` passed a nil \`*checkpointMetadataCache\` to the checkpoint snapshot loader, so the provenance join read each checkpoint's \`metadata.json\` with its own serial \`git cat-file\` subprocess (each with a \`git config -z\` preflight). On this repo that is ~2,200 cat-files, ~4,400 process spawns, ~29ms each. The phase emits no progress, holds the distill pass lock, and is excluded from the \`--json total_seconds\` timer, so it presents as a silent hang.

Root cause confirmed with a goroutine dump mid-hang and a git-exec shim. Details and artifacts: COR-2182.

## What changed

One call site (\`internal/cli/entities_cmd.go\`): load \`export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz\` read-only and pass it to \`loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotLocalOnly\` — the same pattern \`transcript_store.go:233\` already uses. Export remains the cache's only writer. A missing cache file degrades to the previous per-blob reads with identical output.

The cache always exists in the normal flow: distill refuses to run before sessions are exported, and the sessions export builds and saves the cache.

## Numbers (deterministic command agent, jobs 4, isolated brain store)

Full distill, this repo (273 sessions, 1,007 checkpoint roots):

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| wall | 82.7s | 17.0s |
| time to first session distilled | 67.1s | 2.6s |
| git subprocesses | 4,443 | 53 |
| output (facts/chunks/agent calls) | 2590/327/607 | identical |

First-run pipeline (\`refresh sessions\` + first distill), corpus sweep:

| checkpoints / sessions | git-backed before | git-backed after |
|---|---|---|
| 250 / 146 | 47.9s | 34.2s |
| 500 / 178 | 83.9s | 54.1s |
| 1,007 / 273 | 168.7s | 106.0s |

Worst case (cache file deleted): degrades to the old serial scan, identical output.

## Validation

- Focused \`internal/cli\` tests (Distill/Entit/Provenance/metadata-cache/snapshot) pass; gofmt clean.
- Deterministic agent produced identical fact output before/after at three corpus sizes (155/213/326 facts).

## Follow-up (stays on COR-2182)

Export and the COR-2128 transcript reads still exec git per blob; batching via one long-lived \`git cat-file --batch\` process is the next step. After this fix, export is ~70% of first-run time." 2>&1 | tail -5

Ticket updated. Here's the export analysis:

## What `refresh sessions` (the export) does

It builds the brain's session inventory from git: discover every checkpoint, read each one's metadata, pick the latest transcript per session, verify the transcript blobs exist locally, and write the results. Since COR-2128 it copies **no transcript content** — it only produces:

- `manifest.json` → `sources.sessions` (273 sessions: ids, branches, latest checkpoint, virtual transcript paths)
- `export/checkpoint-metadata-cache.json.gz` (the OID-keyed metadata blob cache)

## How it currently works

1. **Discover sources** — `ls-tree -r` on each checkpoint ref (`entire/checkpoints/v1` local + origin, plus per-checkpoint refs): tree listing + OIDs. A handful of git calls; cheap.
2. **Read metadata** — for each of 1,007 checkpoints, read its `metadata.json` (plus per-session sub-metadata) through `checkpointBlobReader`. On a cold cache every read misses → `catFileWithPolicy` → `runCheckpointGitLocal` → **one `git cat-file -p` subprocess per blob**, serial, on the main goroutine. `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` is set per spawn so a partial clone can't phone home (`export.go:680–698`).
3. **Validate transcripts** — `git cat-file -t` per transcript chunk to prove the blob is local (`validateLocalTranscriptSessions`).
4. **Write** manifest + gzip the metadata cache.

## Where the 98.3s goes

| Cost | Measured | Why |
|---|---:|---|
| ~2,483 serial `git cat-file` spawns | ~70–80s | ~30–40ms each; the payload is ~1–3KB of JSON per blob — >95% of each read is process spawn + git startup, not data |
| ~2,501 `git config -z` filter-driver probes | included above | `enumerateRepoFilterDrivers` (the clean/smudge hardening check) runs **once per spawn** instead of once per repo — it doubles the spawn count |
| listings, selection, manifest + cache write | ~10–20s | legitimate work |

Total data actually moved: a few MB. One `git cat-file --batch` process streams that in under a second.

## Proposal

One shared **batch blob reader**, used by export, distill, and the transcript store:

1. Per git dir, spawn one long-lived `git cat-file --batch` child — with the same hardened args (`core.fsmonitor=false`, `core.hooksPath=…`) and `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1`, so the no-egress guarantee is byte-for-byte the one `runCheckpointGitLocal` enforces today. Requests (`<ref>:<path>`) go in on stdin; `<oid> <type> <size>` + content comes back. A sibling `--batch-check` stream replaces the per-chunk `cat-file -t` probes. "missing" responses map onto the existing promisor-absent error path.
2. Integrate at the existing chokepoint — `catFileWithPolicy`, `validateLocalTranscriptSessions`, `readSnapshotTranscriptFromSource` — so all three consumers (export scan, distill transcript reads, transcript store) collapse with one implementation. Keep the per-exec path as fallback if the batch child dies.
3. Memoize the filter-driver probe per repo dir (it's the cheaper half of the win and worth doing even alone).

Expected: export 98s → ~15–25s, distill 38s → ~22s, cold first run **136s → ~40–50s**. Risks to design around: child lifecycle on context cancel, response size caps (reuse the existing read bounds), and not leaking the child in the long-lived MCP server process.

Want me to start building the batch reader?
itsounds reasonable but is this an actual mcp procss? this is jsut spawning the git cli right?

Correct — it's just the git CLI. `git cat-file --batch` is a built-in mode of plain git: the entire-brain binary spawns **one ordinary git child process** via `os/exec` (exactly like it spawns git today) and keeps it alive, writing object names to its stdin and reading blob contents from its stdout. No MCP, no server, no new dependency — the only change is spawning git once per phase instead of 5,000 times.

The MCP mention was about something else: the entire-brain binary itself can run long-lived (as `entire brain mcp`). In that mode the git child's lifecycle needs owning — kill it when the parent's work is done so it doesn't linger. That's a cleanup detail of the design, not part of the transport.

# Review PR

Review a pull request with structured, actionable feedback.

## Arguments

- `this` — PR number, URL, or branch name. If empty, review the current branch's open PR.

## Process

### 1. Fetch PR context

```
gh pr view <pr> --json title,body,baseRefName,headRefName,additions,deletions,changedFiles,commits,author
gh pr diff <pr>
```

Read the PR description carefully — it defines scope and intent. Everything you review should be evaluated against what the PR is trying to accomplish.

### 2. Understand the change

Before reviewing line-by-line:
- What is this PR doing and why?
- What files are touched and what's the blast radius?
- Are there any architectural implications?

### 3. Review with this checklist

**Correctness**
- Does the code do what the PR description says?
- Are there logic errors, off-by-one bugs, or unhandled edge cases?
- Are error paths handled correctly?

**Security**
- Any injection risks (SQL, XSS, command injection)?
- Are secrets, tokens, or credentials handled safely?
- Are inputs validated at system boundaries?

**Testing**
- Are there tests for the new/changed behavior?
- Do tests cover edge cases, not just the happy path?
- Are test assertions meaningful (not just "doesn't throw")?

**Design**
- Does the change follow existing codebase patterns and conventions?
- Is the abstraction level appropriate (not over/under-engineered)?
- Are there unnecessary changes outside the stated scope?

**Performance**
- Any N+1 queries, unbounded loops, or missing pagination?
- Are there opportunities for batching or caching that were missed?
- Will this scale with the data sizes it will encounter?

**Readability**
- Are names clear and consistent with the codebase?
- Is complex logic adequately explained?
- Would a future reader understand the "why" behind non-obvious decisions?

### 4. Adversarial review

Take a second, adversarial pass over the diff. Actively try to break the change — assume it has flaws and hunt for them across:

- **Performance** — worst-case inputs, hot paths, allocations, contention.
- **Stability** — race conditions, partial failures, retries, resource leaks, crash recovery.
- **Correctness** — inputs and states that violate the author's assumptions.
- **Simplicity** — code that could be deleted or replaced with something simpler/stdlib.
- **Platform design standards** — deviations from the platform's established design patterns and conventions.

Add any findings to the output using the same severity format.

### 5. Run /simplify

Run the `/simplify` skill (via the Skill tool) against the changed code and fold its findings into the review output.

### 6. Structure your output

For each finding, use this format:

**[severity] file:line — short title**
Description of the issue and why it matters. Include a suggested fix when possible.

Severity levels:
- **[blocking]** — Must fix before merge. Correctness bugs, security issues, data loss risks.
- **[important]** — Should fix. Design problems, missing tests for critical paths, performance issues.
- **[nit]** — Nice to fix. Style, naming, minor improvements. Don't block merge on these.
- **[question]** — Not necessarily wrong, but needs clarification or discussion.

### 7. Summary

End with a brief summary:
- Overall assessment (approve / request changes / needs discussion)
- What the PR does well
- Top 1-3 items that need attention
- Any scope concerns (changes that seem unrelated to the stated goal)

## Guidelines

- Review what's in the diff, not what you wish was there. Don't request unrelated refactoring.
- If the PR is large, focus on the most impactful files first.
- Be specific — "this could be better" is not useful. Show what "better" looks like.
- Distinguish between "this is wrong" and "I would do this differently." Only the former is blocking.
- If you're unsure about something, use [question] severity instead of asserting it's wrong.
- Read relevant source files (not just the diff) when you need context about how changed code integrates with the rest of the system.

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

Benchmark confirmed after the review refactor: **20.9s total cold first run** (vs 136.2s baseline), identical output (326 facts, 607 calls). Full review report:

## Review findings (all verified; fixes applied in place)

**[blocking] — 2 races, found and fixed**
- `git_catfile_batch.go` — `p.broken` was read outside `p.mu` while another goroutine could write it. Replaced by a self-tombstoning `fail()`; the unsynchronized read no longer exists.
- After restructuring, `-race` caught a second one: the spawn `once` wrote entry fields that `catFileBatchEntryFor` reads under the registry lock. Spawn results are now published under that lock. Both covered by a new 8-goroutine concurrency test run with `-race`.

**[important] — 5, fixed**
- Registry mutex was held across child spawn (including a `git config` probe exec), blocking cache hits on other keys. Spawn now happens in a per-entry `sync.Once` outside the lock.
- A persistently failing child degraded into a spawn storm (probe + spawn + failed round-trip + per-exec fallback, per read — worse than pre-change). Failing keys now tombstone for a 1-minute cooldown and answer fast errors that route callers straight to per-exec.
- The spawn preamble hand-copied the runner's hardening chokepoint, making `git_harden.go`'s "single spawn point" invariant false. Extracted `hardenedGitInvocation` into `runner.go`; the buffered runner, streaming runner, and batch child all consume it (this also deleted a pre-existing third copy in `Stream`).
- Concrete `ExecRunner` type switch replaced with the package's optional-capability idiom: `GitCatFileBatcher` interface alongside `EnvironmentCommandRunner`/`CommandStreamer`, so wrappers opt in deliberately.
- Child stderr was discarded (a broken child reported only "read header: EOF") and `WaitDelay` was missing. Now uses the runner's `cappedBuffer`; cooldown errors carry the child's stderr.

**[nit] — 4, fixed:** whitespace specs no longer kill a healthy child (routed to per-exec); oversize reads kill-and-fall-back instead of draining a 1GiB record; the local-only env is produced by one `localOnlyGitEnv()` shared with `runCheckpointGitLocal`; tests reuse the existing `liveGit` fixture and the parity tests now genuinely compare batch vs per-exec via a non-batch runner.

**Noted, deliberately not done (on COR-2182 as follow-ups):**
- Body reads serialize on one child per key where per-exec allowed 4 parallel decompressions — measured cost is nil here (extraction wait 2.6s); a child pool is the option if a corpus ever shows contention.
- Three remaining per-object exec loops (`partitionPresentCommits`, `verifyCommitUncached`, `entityindex.isGraftedBoundary`) could use the reader later; the last needs the capability exported cross-package.
- Kept the separate `--batch-check` child (one reviewer suggested merging): type probes must not stream multi-MB transcript bodies just to learn "blob" — now documented on the key type.

## Summary

**Approve.** The change does what it claims — cold first run 136.2s → 20.9s (6.5×), zero per-blob git spawns, byte-identical outputs at three corpus sizes — and after this pass the wiring sits at the right depth: one hardened spawn point, capability-based opt-in, bounded failure behavior. Verified: `-race` on the new suite, full Export/Transcript/Distill/Snapshot/Checkpoint/Entity/Runner/Stream/Harden suites pass, gofmt clean, benchmark re-run post-refactor.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/evisdrenova/.claude/plugins/cache/entire-skills/entire/0.7.2/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

content.text:
Finding `01M5AX5BKREDDFCJG8MDNG6R3E` (medium) fixed and resolved.

- **The problem:** `request` held `p.mu` through blocking reads with no cancellation — a stalled child (lazy fetch on the non-local-only key in a partial clone, or a wedged git) would hang the caller past its deadline and queue every other caller on the key.
- **The fix** (`internal/cli/git_catfile_batch.go`): a `context.AfterFunc` watcher kills the child the moment the caller's ctx ends; the blocked read unblocks with an error, the existing `fail()` path tombstones the key (later callers go per-exec), and the returned error joins `ctx.Err()` so callers see the deadline, not an opaque pipe error. The rare benign race — ctx ending just as a request completes — kills a healthy child, which simply respawns; that's documented at the watcher.
- **Test:** `TestCatFileBatchStalledChildIsKilledAtDeadline` drives a never-answering child (`sh -c 'cat > /dev/null'`) against a 100ms deadline and asserts `context.DeadlineExceeded`, no hang, and the broken mark. Full batch suite passes under `-race`; gofmt clean.

Changes are uncommitted on `cor-2182-catfile-batch` for your review — say push and I'll put it on the trail.

Profile complete. Here's where the remaining **18.5s** of the full-size first distill goes (wall 18.5s; 27.9s total CPU including agent subprocesses; Go process itself 13.2s):

| Bucket | Time | What it is |
|---|---:|---|
| **Reconcile** | 7.3s | 280 serial agent calls × ~26ms — with the command agent this is pure `python3` startup; with a real agent it's model latency |
| **Transcript preprocessing** | ~5.0s CPU | `preprocessTranscriptForDistill` (38% of Go CPU): JSON-decoding 1.69GB of raw JSONL to strip tool I/O down to 26MB |
| **GC/allocator churn** | ~4–5s CPU | `memclr`/`madvise`/`memmove` — fallout from preprocessing's allocations (1.2GB peak RSS); shrinks if preprocessing shrinks |
| **Extraction wait** | 2.6s | 327 agent calls at jobs=4 — subprocess startup, parallelized |
| Transcript reads (batch pipe) | 1.7s | `transcriptStore.Read` through the cat-file child — already cheap |
| Fact writes | 0.2s | |

(Prefetch CPU overlaps the agent calls, so the buckets sum past wall — the engine is pipelined now.)

**What this means for the next optimization:**

1. **Reconcile serialization (7.3s) is the biggest wall-clock lever** — but it's deliberately serial ("reconcile and fact application keep their exact serial semantics" per the pipeline's design comment), so overlapping it means relaxing ordering, e.g. reconciling independent branches/paths concurrently. Real-agent users feel this strongest since each call is an LLM round-trip.
2. **Preprocessing (~5s CPU + the GC it drags)** is the honest CLI-side win: it fully re-decodes every transcript as generic JSON on every full run. Levers: stream-parse and skip non-text fields without materializing maps, or persist the stripped text keyed by content hash (~26MB cache) so forced/full runs don't re-strip unchanged sessions.
3. Extraction wait is near-irreducible for the command agent and model-bound for real agents.

One caveat worth stating: with the deterministic test agent, ~10s of the 18.5s is literally `python3` interpreter startup (607 spawns). A real-agent distill replaces that with model latency, so from here on, CLI-side optimization should target #2 (pure CLI cost) and the reconcile *structure* (#1), not the agent spawn itself.

content.text:
Here's the full pipeline, stage by stage, with what each one consumes, produces, and costs (times from the profile, full corpus, deterministic agent):

## 0. Export (`refresh sessions`) — before distill can run — *1.3s*

Walks the checkpoint branch (`entire/checkpoints/v1`), reads each checkpoint's `metadata.json` (now via the batch reader), and writes the **session inventory** into the brain manifest: 273 sessions, each with its branch, latest checkpoint, and a *virtual* transcript path pointing into git. No transcript content is copied (COR-2128). Also writes the metadata-blob cache.

## 1. Plan — *sub-second*

Distill loads the manifest, takes the pass lock (one distill per brain at a time), builds the provenance resolvers, and computes a **cache salt** — a hash of the prompts, agent, chunk size, and threshold. Each session gets a fingerprint keyed by that salt; a session whose fingerprint matches the previous run's is **skipped entirely** (that's why incremental re-distills are cheap). `--force` ignores the cache.

## 2. Prefetch — read, strip, chunk — *~7s of CPU, overlapped* 

A producer pipeline prepares sessions in chronological order, a few in flight:

- **Read** the transcript from git through the cat-file batch child (*1.7s*).
- **Preprocess** (*5.0s CPU — the biggest pure-CLI cost*): JSON-decode the raw JSONL (1.69GB total) and strip tool calls, tool outputs, and meta records, keeping only the conversation text the agent should see — 1.69GB → 26MB. The fingerprint is taken over this *stripped* text, so churn confined to tool I/O doesn't invalidate the cache.
- **Chunk** the stripped text into ≤256KB pieces (327 chunks across 273 sessions; most sessions are one chunk).
- **Dispatch** each chunk's extraction call into a shared pool, up to `--jobs` in flight *across* sessions.

## 3. Extraction — one agent call per chunk — *2.6s wait, parallel*

Each chunk goes to the agent (codex/claude-code/ollama/command) with the distill prompt: *"read this transcript chunk, output durable facts"* — one fact per line with a taxonomy path (`architecture.*`, `workflow.*`, …), text, and kind. Output is parsed into candidate `factRecord`s, each **anchored** to its provenance (session, checkpoint, commit, transcript line), sharpened by the entity index where it can place the fact on a specific commit. 327 calls here produced 326 facts.

## 4. Reconcile — one agent call per fact-bearing chunk — *7.3s, serial*

This is the dedup/conflict stage, and the reason facts don't pile up as near-duplicates:

- For the chunk's candidates, collect the **existing active facts at the same taxonomy paths** on that branch (capped at the 50 most recent).
- **Shortcut:** if there are none, every candidate is `new` — **no agent call**. That's why only 280 of 327 chunks paid a reconcile call.
- Otherwise, send the agent two numbered lists on stdin — `CANDIDATES` and `EXISTING` — and ask for one decision per candidate: **`new`** (nothing like it), **`merge`** (restatement of existing fact N — consolidate), or **`supersede`** (contradicts/replaces fact N), each with a confidence. The prompt is explicit that "use tabs" vs "use spaces" is a *supersede*, not a *merge*.
- **Apply with a threshold:** decisions at or above `--confidence` (0.75) are applied automatically; below it, the pair is queued as a **proposal** for human review (`facts review`). In `--newest-first` backfills, supersede is *never* auto-applied — extraction order isn't evidence of recency, so both facts are kept for review.
- If the reconcile agent fails, candidates are stored as `new` with a warning — failure adds duplicates, never loses facts.

It's serial by design: each chunk's decisions must see the fact set as updated by the previous chunk, or two chunks could both "merge into" a fact the other just superseded.

## 5. Write — *0.2s*

Facts land in per-branch stores, flushed periodically (so a killed run keeps its progress) and finally under the brain write lock: fact files, taxonomy, proposals queue, and the manifest summary (`sources.facts` — the JSON you see with `--json`). Sessions whose chunks all succeeded get their fingerprint cached as "distilled"; a failed session stays uncached so the next run retries it.

---

**Cost map against the 18.5s:** reconcile 7.3s (serial agent latency — spawn cost for the test agent, model latency for a real one) · preprocessing ~5s CPU + ~4s of GC it causes · extraction wait 2.6s (parallel) · reads 1.7s · writes 0.2s. The two levers that are purely ours: stream/caching the preprocessing, and relaxing reconcile's serialization (its ordering constraint is per-branch-per-path, which is what any safe parallelization would have to preserve).

All three answered from the code (plus a Brain recall for recorded rationale — none exists on these, so what follows is from source, not recorded decisions):

## 2. Prefetch — isn't the saved transcript already stripped?

Partially, by design — but this corpus doesn't benefit:

- At checkpoint time the CLI **does** write a normalized `transcript.jsonl` ("compact") beside the raw `full.jsonl`, and export prefers it. But the switch is **all-or-nothing** per export (`useCompactTranscripts`, `export.go:1898`): one manifest carries one `transcript_mode`, so if *any* exported session lacks a compact pointer — compaction is best-effort, and anything written by an older CLI has none — the **whole export falls back to raw**. Our export warned exactly that: 754 entries missing → everything shipped as raw `full.jsonl`.
- Even compact isn't distill-ready: `preprocessTranscriptForDistill` strips tool calls/outputs/meta records while **preserving line numbers** (each dropped record becomes a blank line) so a fact's provenance anchor still points at the right line in the original transcript. On compact input it's cheap; on raw it's the 5s we measured.
- **And yes — streaming is exactly the right fix.** Today it buffers the whole blob, splits lines, and `json.Unmarshal`s every line into `map[string]any` (that generic decode is most of the CPU and the 1.2GB RSS). The batch reader already hands us a pipe; stripping and chunking line-by-line as it reads, with a targeted token scan instead of full maps, keeps the line-number invariant and kills both the CPU and the GC churn. The deeper fix is making the compact fallback **per-session** instead of all-or-nothing (or backfilling compact transcripts), so most sessions skip heavy stripping entirely.

## 3. Why the ollama interface?

No recorded rationale in Brain (empty recall — doesn't prove there wasn't one). What the code shows: it's the **no-egress local-model option** — a deliberately hardened client that only talks to `127.0.0.1:11434/api/generate`, rejects non-loopback URLs, redirects, and proxies (`distill_cmd.go:2517-2560`), with a retained CI contract proving it can't leak. Ollama is the most common local runtime, so it's a reasonable default — but you're right that it's not universal: LM Studio, llama.cpp's server, vLLM, and mlx all speak the **OpenAI-compatible** `/v1/chat/completions` instead (and ollama itself also exposes that). The clean generalization is one loopback-hardened OpenAI-compatible agent (`--agent local --model … --url http://127.0.0.1:<port>/v1`) that covers all of them, keeping `ollama` as an alias. Today the escape hatch for anything else is `--agent command` (any argv, stdin→stdout).

## 4. Reconcile — don't we skip already-processed transcripts?

We do, and the ordering is what you'd hope:

- **Fingerprint check comes first**, before the transcript is even read (`cachedCheckpointDistill` in the prefetch producer). A cached session costs zero reads, zero preprocessing, zero agent calls — its prior facts are retained as-is. That's why incremental distills are fast.
- Checkpoints are immutable, so "changed" means **new checkpoints appended** — which changes the session's fingerprint and triggers re-distill of just that session. The fingerprint hashes the *stripped* text, so tool-output churn alone doesn't invalidate it.
- **So why reconcile at all?** Because the cache only prevents re-extracting *the same transcript*. Reconcile solves a different problem: **different sessions producing overlapping or contradicting facts**. Forty sessions each independently mention "we use testify" — without reconcile you store forty near-duplicates. A later session records "we switched from X to Y" — supersede retires the old fact instead of serving both forever. That's cross-session semantic dedup and contradiction handling, which no transcript-level cache can do; it also runs *within* a first full distill as facts accumulate chunk by chunk.
- It's already partially lazy: a chunk whose taxonomy paths have **no existing facts** skips the agent call entirely (47 of our 327 chunks did). The next cheapening lever is an embedding-similarity prefilter so the agent is only consulted when something at those paths is actually close.

## Why strip at all?

It's not a leftover — it's what keeps the agent step affordable. But your instinct about the *disparate passes* is right. Separate the two:

**The strip itself earns its keep, for three reasons:**

1. **It's a 65× reduction in what the agent reads.** Raw transcripts are 1.69GB; the conversation text the agent actually mines is 26MB. Tool calls, tool outputs, file dumps, and diffs are ~98.5% of the bytes and carry almost no durable facts. Without stripping, 327 extraction calls become ~21,000, every one billed at real-model token prices — the strip *is* the cost control, independent of where transcripts live.
2. **Chunks must fit a model context** (`--max-chunk-bytes`, with the 32K-context ollama warning). Unstripped, each chunk would be mostly tool spam with a sliver of conversation — worse facts *and* more chunks.
3. **The cache fingerprint hashes the stripped text**, deliberately: tool-I/O churn in a re-exported transcript doesn't invalidate a session's distill cache. Hash the raw bytes and trivial churn re-distills everything.

**What *is* vestigial is the shape, exactly as you suspect.** The current flow is: read the whole blob into a string → split into lines → `json.Unmarshal` every line into a `map[string]any` → rejoin → hash → cache-check → chunk. That read-everything-then-pass-over-it structure is an artifact of the materialized-file days (`readCanonicalHistoryTranscript` returning `[]byte`). Nothing requires it. The streaming version is what you said:

> stream from the batch-reader pipe → per line, a cheap token peek ("is this a tool record?") instead of a full map decode → kept text goes into a hash-writer + a small stripped buffer → fingerprint ready at EOF → cache-check → chunk straight from the stripped buffer → dispatch.

One pass, no 1.69GB string, no per-line maps, no 1.2GB RSS. The only real constraint is ordering: the fingerprint must be complete before the cache decision, so you buffer the *stripped* text (small) rather than the raw. And once compact transcripts fall back **per-session** instead of all-or-nothing, most sessions arrive pre-normalized and the strip degrades to a passthrough — the comment in `preprocessTranscriptForDistill` already anticipates that ("lines that are not JSON objects… are passed through unchanged").

So: keep the strip, kill the passes. That's the ~5s CPU + ~4s GC from the profile, and it's pure CLI cost — real wins regardless of which agent runs.

On 4 — fair to stay skeptical; the honest test would be measuring how many duplicates/contradictions reconcile actually catches on this corpus (merge/supersede counts are in the summary: 6 supersedes + the merges behind 326-from-607-chunks), and whether a cheap similarity prefilter could skip most of its 280 calls. We can quantify that when we get to it.

content.text:
**Implemented and validated — honest verdict: big CPU win, small wall win.** The pipeline overlap we built earlier means preprocessing was already hidden behind agent calls, so the stopwatch barely moves:

| Full-corpus `--force` distill | map-based (merged main) | attempt 1: typed `RawMessage` | **attempt 2: token walker** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| wall | 18.5s | 22.7s ❌ | **17.8–18.1s** |
| engine `total_seconds` | 17.7s | 21.8s | **17.0–17.4s** |
| Go process CPU (user) | ~17.4s | 17.7s | **13.9s (−20%)** |
| peak RSS | 1.20GB | 1.20GB | 1.19GB |
| output / fingerprints | — | identical | **identical** |

What happened, in order:

1. **Attempt 1 (typed `json.RawMessage` fields) was a regression** — the profile showed why: `RawMessage` *copies* its subtree, and the giant tool outputs live inside the kept fields (`message.content[].content`), so we copied them 2–3× before discarding. Caught it by measuring, not shipping.
2. **Attempt 2 is a `jsontext` token walker**: streams tokens, captures only the candidate strings, `SkipValue`s everything else with zero allocation, v1-compat options (duplicate keys, invalid UTF-8). Line slices are zero-copy; only the rare document-form (opencode) transcript pays a string conversion.
3. **Byte-identical output proven three ways**: a differential test against the legacy implementation (kept verbatim as reference) across ~50 trap cases — it caught one real divergence (a bare `null` line) before CI ever saw it; corpus-exact parity (26,246,044 preprocessed bytes, byte-for-byte); and 273/273 cache hits when the new binary re-distills an old-binary brain. **No fingerprint invalidation, no re-distill for users.**
4. RSS didn't move because the raw blobs are still fully buffered by the transcript store (the checkpoint reader assembles chunks in memory); true streaming-from-the-pipe is a store-level change.

**Why wall didn't drop:** the prefetcher already overlaps preprocessing with agent calls, so the 3.5s of saved CPU was mostly hidden. The savings are real for battery/CI/loaded machines and shrink GC pressure, but the wall clock is now firmly bound by **reconcile (9.0–9.4s, serial)** — exactly the next lever we identified.

All distill/export/transcript test families pass; race-clean; gofmt clean. Changes are uncommitted in this workspace.

Your call on direction: ship this as a CPU/efficiency win (it's safe and well-tested), or set it aside and go straight at reconcile, which is where the remaining wall time actually lives?
hm it seems like then it's not worth it? thoughts?

My honest take: **drop it.** The data says so, and so does the kind of code it is.

- **The win nobody feels:** 0.5s of wall on an 18s run — within noise. The 20% CPU saving is real but invisible because the prefetcher already hides preprocessing behind agent latency. CPU-only wins matter when something is CPU-bound; this pipeline isn't, and with a real agent it's even less so.
- **The cost is permanent:** ~350 lines of subtle token-walker code whose correctness depends on staying byte-identical with a reference copy. Every future transcript dialect now gets added in three places (walker, legacy reference, differential table) instead of one easy map-based switch. That's a tax on every future contributor for a win the stopwatch can't see.
- **The right trigger to resurrect it exists and hasn't fired:** if reconcile gets parallelized and someone runs a fast local model at high `--jobs`, preprocessing could become the bottleneck — *then* this is worth its complexity, and we now know exactly how to do it safely (token walk + differential parity + the cache-hit proof).

What we bought with the afternoon isn't the code, it's the knowledge: preprocessing is fully overlapped, the wall is reconcile-bound, byte-parity is achievable without invalidating fingerprints, and `RawMessage`-typed decoding is a trap (it *copies* subtrees). That's worth banking even if the diff isn't.

So my recommendation: revert the working tree, save the patch for later resurrection, record the findings on COR-2182 and in Brain, and go after **reconcile** — the 9s that's actually on the clock. Want me to do that?

content.text:
No recorded prior attempts to change it (only the in-code rationale), so here's the design, grounded in how reconcile actually works:

## Why it's serial today

Each chunk's reconcile compares its candidates against **the branch's current active facts at the candidates' taxonomy paths** (`activeFactsAtPaths`, capped at 50), and its decisions are applied *before* the next chunk's reconcile runs. That ordering is load-bearing: if chunk A adds "use tabs" and chunk B extracted "use spaces", B's reconcile must see A's fact to emit `supersede`. Run them against the same snapshot concurrently and both come back `new` — you've stored the contradiction reconcile exists to prevent.

But note what the dependency actually is: **a chunk only reads and writes facts at its own candidates' paths.** Two chunks whose path sets don't intersect are provably independent. That's the opening.

## The fix, two parts

**Part 1 — similarity prefilter (biggest win, smallest change).** Today there's already a shortcut: no existing facts at the candidate's paths → auto-`new`, no agent call (47 of 327 chunks took it). Extend it semantically: the brain ships a bundled embedder (the model2vec engine recall already uses). Before calling the agent, embed the candidates and the existing facts at their paths; if nothing is within a similarity threshold, auto-`new` without the call. The agent is only consulted when something is actually *close* enough that merge/supersede is plausible. Failure direction is safe — it's the same direction as today's agent-failure fallback (worst case: a duplicate is stored, and `facts review`/`gc` exist). For real-agent users this is the entire ballgame: 280 LLM round-trips (5–15 min at 1–3s each) become a few dozen.

**Part 2 — path-disjoint concurrency for the calls that remain.** A small scheduler in the consumer: before dispatching a chunk's reconcile, acquire locks for its candidate paths (sorted acquisition, no deadlock); release after `applyFactActions`. Disjoint chunks reconcile in parallel; chunks contending on the same path serialize exactly as today, in chunk order. Semantics are preserved by construction — the only facts a reconcile reads are at paths it holds locked. Branches are already independent fact sets, so cross-branch parallelism is free.

## What it buys, honestly

- **Deterministic test agent:** 9s → maybe 3–5s. Parallelism is capped by path contention — 326 facts cluster into relatively few taxonomy paths, so popular paths (`workflow.*`, `architecture.*`) will still serialize. Modest.
- **Real agent (the case that matters):** the prefilter dominates — most of the 280 round-trips disappear outright, and the rest overlap. That's minutes off a real first distill, which is where users actually feel this.

One caveat to design around: the prefilter changes *behavior* (some merges the agent would have caught become duplicates until the next pass), unlike everything we shipped today, which was byte-identical. So it wants a threshold chosen against measured data — the corpus gives us ground truth, since we know the agent's actual merge/supersede decisions for all 280 calls and can measure what recall a given threshold achieves — plus a flag to disable it. Part 2 alone is semantics-preserving if you want a pure-speed first step.

That's the shape. It's parked as the open item on COR-2182 whenever you want to pick it up.

input.title: Distill reconcile is serial: add a similarity prefilter and path-disjoint concurrency
input.description:
## Problem

After COR-2182, reconcile is the dominant wall-clock cost of a full distill: ~9s of a ~22s run with the deterministic command agent (280 serial agent calls at ~30ms each). With a real agent each call is an LLM round-trip, so the same 280 calls are 5–15 minutes — the biggest cost a real user feels in a first distill.

It is serial by design: a chunk's reconcile compares its candidates against the branch's **current** active facts at the candidates' taxonomy paths (`reconcileChunkCandidates`, `internal/cli/reconcile.go:329`), and its decisions apply before the next chunk runs. Chunk A adds "use tabs"; chunk B's "use spaces" must see A's fact to emit `supersede`. Concurrent reconciles against one snapshot would both answer `new` and store the contradiction reconcile exists to prevent.

The real dependency is narrower than "serial": a chunk only reads/writes facts at **its own candidates' paths**. Chunks with disjoint path sets are independent.

## Fix, two parts

**1. Similarity prefilter (biggest win, smallest change).** Extend the existing shortcut (no facts at the candidate's paths → auto-`new`, no agent call; 47 of 327 chunks took it on the benchmark corpus). Embed candidates and the existing facts at their paths with the bundled model2vec embedder; if nothing is within a similarity threshold, auto-`new` without the agent call. Consult the agent only when something is close enough that merge/supersede is plausible. Failure direction is safe — same as today's agent-failure fallback (a duplicate is stored; `facts review`/`facts gc` exist). For real agents this removes most of the 280 round-trips outright.

Caveat: unlike COR-2182's changes this is NOT byte-identical behavior — some merges the agent would have caught become duplicates until a later pass. Pick the threshold against ground truth: the benchmark corpus has the agent's actual decisions for all 280 calls, so a threshold's recall of merge/supersede decisions is directly measurable. Ship behind a flag with a disable switch.

**2. Path-disjoint concurrency (semantics-preserving).** A small scheduler in the distill consumer: acquire locks for a chunk's candidate taxonomy paths (sorted acquisition) before its reconcile, release after `applyFactActions`. Disjoint chunks reconcile in parallel; contending chunks serialize in chunk order exactly as today. Correct by construction — a reconcile only touches facts at paths it holds. Branches are separate fact sets, so cross-branch parallelism is free. This part alone is a pure-speed change with unchanged output if the prefilter is deemed too risky.

## Expected

- Command agent: reconcile ~9s → ~3–5s (bounded by path contention: 326 facts cluster in few popular paths).
- Real agent: the prefilter dominates — most round-trips disappear; the remainder overlap. Minutes off a real first distill.

## Context

Benchmarks, profiles, and the pipeline walkthrough live on COR-2182 (distill is now: export ~1s constant; distill scales with session count; reconcile is the top in-engine cost at 9.0–9.6s, extraction wait 2.6s, writes 0.2s). Brain facts: `architecture.distill.bottleneck`, `architecture.distill.preprocessing`.
